title: Two Plans for Residential Food-Waste Collection
description: Synthesize two implementation plans with health and budget evidence to judge participation, cost, and operational tradeoffs.
subject: rla
passage:
PLAN A - Weekly Curbside Collection

The sanitation department proposes giving households sealed food-scrap bins and collecting them every week on the same day as trash. A route simulation estimates that adding food-waste pickup would increase collection-driving time by 11 percent. The regional compost facility has capacity for the projected material. In a phone survey of 760 households, 58 percent said curbside pickup would make them more likely to separate food scraps than a system requiring them to travel to a drop-off point.

The department estimates the first-year program would cost $1.3 million, including bins, trucks, labor, and outreach. Staff expect later annual costs to decline after the one-time bin purchase. The plan includes a six-month pilot in two neighborhoods before citywide expansion.

PLAN B - Neighborhood Drop-Off Hubs

A sustainability advisory group proposes twelve staffed drop-off hubs located at libraries, markets, and community centers. Residents would bring food scraps during open hours. The group estimates first-year costs of $620,000 because the city would need fewer collection routes and could use larger shared containers. It cites a pilot at two farmers' markets where 1,900 households registered to use food-scrap drop-off over four months.

However, registration did not measure how often each household actually delivered scraps, and the farmers' market locations served neighborhoods with relatively high car ownership. The advisory group proposes placing several new hubs near bus routes and apartment complexes to improve access.

PUBLIC HEALTH MEMO

Health staff say either system can control odor and pests if containers are sealed, collection/emptying is frequent enough, and cleaning rules are followed. They caution that unattended shared containers can create problems if they overflow, while household bins can create problems if residents store them improperly. The memo recommends tracking contamination, odor complaints, missed collections, and participation under whichever system is tested.

BUDGET OFFICE NOTE

The budget office says the plans should not be compared only by first-year cost. Curbside collection may produce higher participation but higher route costs; hubs may be cheaper but could shift time and transportation burdens onto residents. The office recommends reporting cost per participating household and cost per ton of correctly separated food waste after comparable pilot periods.

Both planning teams agree that participation will probably change as residents become familiar with the program. For that reason, staff recommend reporting monthly trends rather than judging either pilot only from its first weeks. They also want identical definitions for a participating household and for correctly separated material so that the two pilots cannot appear different merely because they count success differently.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest evidence advantage of Plan A over Plan B regarding expected household participation?
questions.explanation: Plan A has evidence tied directly to the convenience choice, while Plan B's registration figure is a weaker proxy for sustained participation.
questions.rule: Compare not just numbers, but what each number actually measures.

options.text: Plan A is more expensive.
options.whyWrong: Higher cost does not establish higher participation.

options.text: The household survey directly asks about curbside versus travel-to-drop-off convenience, while Plan B's market registration does not show actual repeated use.
Plan A uses sealed containers.
options.whyWrong: The health memo says either system can control problems with proper containers and operations.

options.text: Plan A has already operated citywide for a year.
options.whyWrong: It is still proposed with a pilot.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest evidence advantage of Plan B over Plan A?
questions.explanation: The cost estimate is relevant to affordability, while the note correctly preserves the need to compare cost with participation and collected material.
questions.rule: A relevant advantage is not automatically sufficient to decide the whole policy.

options.text: Its estimated first-year cost is substantially lower, though that figure does not by itself establish better overall value.
Its registration figure proves every household participated every week.
options.whyWrong: Registration does not measure frequency of use.

options.text: Drop-off hubs cannot create odor problems.
options.whyWrong: The health memo warns that overflowing shared containers can create problems.

options.text: Car ownership is high in every neighborhood.
options.whyWrong: The passage identifies high car ownership as a limitation of the earlier market locations.

questions.prompt: Which limitation most weakens using the farmers' market pilot to predict citywide hub participation?
questions.explanation: Both sample context and outcome measurement make it risky to treat registration as a citywide participation rate.
questions.rule: Check whether the pilot population resembles the target population and whether the measure matches the claimed behavior.

options.text: The pilot used shared containers.
options.whyWrong: That is part of the proposed model and not the main transfer problem.

options.text: The registered households came from locations with relatively high car ownership, and registration did not measure repeated actual use.
The pilot lasted four months, which makes all of its data invalid.
options.whyWrong: Duration alone does not invalidate the evidence.

options.text: The city has libraries.
options.whyWrong: Library locations do not resolve the representativeness and usage-measurement limits.

questions.prompt: How does the public health memo affect the debate?
questions.explanation: The memo reframes sanitation as an implementation-quality issue and gives measurable outcomes for either pilot.
questions.rule: A third source can clarify which disagreement is real and which is based on a false either/or.

options.text: It proves Plan A is the only sanitary option.
options.whyWrong: The memo says either system can control odor and pests with proper management.

options.text: It proves Plan B is the only sanitary option.
options.whyWrong: The memo also identifies overflow risks for shared containers.

options.text: It shifts the question from whether one container type is automatically safe to how well either system manages sealing, frequency, cleaning, and operational failures.
It makes participation evidence irrelevant.
options.whyWrong: Sanitation and participation are separate criteria that both matter.

questions.prompt: Which metric proposed by the budget office is most useful for comparing value when participation rates differ?
questions.explanation: This metric relates spending to a meaningful program output and allows systems with different participation levels to be compared.
questions.rule: For value comparisons, pair cost with the outcome the program is trying to produce.

options.text: Total first-year cost alone.
options.whyWrong: A cheaper program could collect far less useful material; total cost lacks an outcome denominator.

options.text: Number of containers purchased.
options.whyWrong: Container count is an input, not a direct value measure.

options.text: Cost per ton of correctly separated food waste.
Number of libraries in the city.
options.whyWrong: Library count does not combine program cost and successful waste diversion.

questions.prompt: Which pilot design would best allow the city to choose between the plans?
questions.explanation: Comparable populations, periods, and shared outcomes would let the city distinguish program effects from neighborhood differences and compare both value and usability.
questions.rule: A fair comparison controls obvious differences and measures the same decision criteria for each option.

options.text: Test curbside in one type of neighborhood and hubs in a very different type, then compare raw totals only.
options.whyWrong: Different populations could explain the outcome differences.

options.text: Run comparable pilots in matched neighborhoods, track actual participating households, correctly separated tons, full operating costs, access patterns, contamination, and complaints for the same period.
Choose the lower first-year estimate without testing participation.
options.whyWrong: This ignores the budget office's warning that cost and participation must be evaluated together.

options.text: Ask only residents who already compost which plan they prefer.
options.whyWrong: That sample would not represent residents whose behavior the program needs to change.

questions.prompt: Which additional evidence would be MOST relevant to deciding whether Plan B’s lower first-year cost would remain an advantage after the program is widely used?
questions.explanation: The decision concerns whether the apparent cost advantage survives wider use, so the most relevant evidence compares operating costs at matched participation levels.
questions.rule: Relevant evidence must answer the exact uncertainty in the claim, not merely relate to the general topic.

options.text: A list of the colors available for food-waste collection containers.
options.whyWrong: Container color does not address whether operating costs remain lower at larger scale.

options.text: A survey asking residents whether they think food waste is unpleasant.
options.whyWrong: General attitudes do not measure the cost consequences of wider program use.

options.text: The number of grocery stores in neighborhoods outside the pilot area.
options.whyWrong: Store count does not directly test Plan B’s operating cost at higher participation.

options.text: Projected collection, staffing, and overflow-management costs at several participation levels, compared with Plan A’s costs at the same levels.

curriculum.learningObjective: Evaluate claims, evidence, reasoning, and multiple sources under GED-style conditions.
